display: Linda, a freelance Cantonese–English court interpreter in New York (also Mandarin; I understand Taishanese through my grandmother), looking for ways to put my language skills to use.

signals.text: I want to record my grandmother's Taishanese stories and words before they are lost, and I don't know the best way to do it.
I'm looking for people who work on Taishanese or Toishanese, such as linguists, archivists or community projects, so the recordings I'm making end up somewhere useful.
My court bookings have dropped by about a third since remote interpreting expanded.
I have a lot of free evenings now, and I used to spend them preparing for cases.
I'm deciding whether to move fully into remote interpreting or look for a different line of work that uses the same skills.
Remote agency rates are far below what I earn in court, and I'm unsure the move is worth it.
Many interpreters I know are worried about the same shift, and I'd like to compare notes with others in the field.
I'm thinking of taking my grandmother back to her home village in Taishan next spring, and I'd like advice from anyone who has travelled with an elderly relative.
I'm learning pottery and I'm still bad at it. I'd like to meet other beginners and talk about it.
I feel nostalgic for the Chinatown I grew up in, and many of the old shops are gone.
My family is going through a big change with the family business and property, and I'm still working out how I feel about it.
I wish I spent more time with my grandmother and had more chances to speak Cantonese with her.
I'm lonelier than I expected on free evenings and would welcome low-pressure company.

offers.text: Court-certified Cantonese–English interpreting for legal, family and housing matters, in person or remote.
Fluent Cantonese, Mandarin and English, and I understand Taishanese and Toishan-flavoured Cantonese.
Glossaries of legal and medical vocabulary in Cantonese and English that I built over years of work.
Interpreter training from Hunter College and experience in the court interpreter profession, which I can share with newcomers.
Help with medical or legal appointments for Cantonese or Taishanese speakers, as I've done for my grandmother since childhood.
A quiet home office with a good headset and a second laptop, set up for remote sessions.
Free evenings for translation, transcription, tutoring or language projects, outside Thursday nights.
Access to an 89-year-old native Taishanese speaker, my grandmother, who is willing to tell stories and share words.
I know Chinatown and the Flushing community well, having grown up on Mott Street.

catchers.hypo: I'm a linguist documenting Toishanese and I'm looking for native speakers who can record vocabulary and stories.
catchers.can: Linda can introduce her grandmother, who speaks Taishanese, and help interpret and transcribe the sessions, if her grandmother agrees.
catchers.confirm: Is your project documenting Taishanese or Toishanese speech in a way that credits the speakers and keeps recordings with the family?

catchers.hypo: Our small law office needs a Cantonese–English interpreter for client meetings and document reviews, mostly on evenings or by video.
catchers.can: Linda can take interpreting work in evening or video slots, within her confidentiality limits.
catchers.confirm: Does the work pay at least $35 an hour and fit outside weekday court hours?

catchers.hypo: I'm a clinic administrator and many of our elderly patients speak Cantonese or Taishanese. Do you know who could help us communicate better?
catchers.can: Linda can interpret or review patient materials, and she can train staff on language and cultural issues.
catchers.confirm: Do you need Cantonese or Taishanese help in a medical setting, and are you able to pay a professional rate?

catchers.hypo: I'm an interpreter whose bookings are down too. How have you adapted to remote work, and which agencies pay well?
catchers.can: Linda can compare notes on remote interpreting, agency rates and experience.
catchers.confirm: Are you a working court or community interpreter looking to share information about the field?

catchers.hypo: I took my elderly mother back to a village near Taishan last year. Would you like to know how we planned it?
catchers.can: Linda can use practical advice about travelling to Guangzhou and Taishan with an elderly relative, and she may be able to share her own plans.
catchers.confirm: Have you travelled to Taishan or nearby areas with an elderly family member who has limited mobility?

catchers.hypo: I run a beginner pottery group in Brooklyn and we're looking for new members who don't mind making ugly bowls.
catchers.can: Linda can join an extra class or meetup, though her Thursday class is protected.
catchers.confirm: Does your group meet on a day other than Thursday, and is it open to beginners?

catchers.hypo: Our Chinese-American community oral-history project is collecting stories from older immigrants in Cantonese and Taishanese.
catchers.can: Linda can help with Cantonese and Taishanese-flavoured interviews and transcription, and she can introduce older relatives or acquaintances.
catchers.confirm: Do you interview older immigrants in Cantonese or Taishanese and have a consent process for recordings?

catchers.hypo: My father runs a small family shop in Chinatown and we want to turn our recipes and stories into a bilingual record before we sell. Who could help?
catchers.can: Linda knows what it is like to grow up in a Chinatown family business and could help with bilingual translation, listening and ideas.
catchers.confirm: Are you looking for bilingual translation or advice from someone with a Chinatown family-business background, and do you have a budget?

catchers.hypo: I'm a Cantonese speaker living alone in the city and I'd like language practice and company on weeknight evenings.
catchers.can: Linda can offer conversation practice and company in Cantonese on evenings other than Thursday, and her friend Jen's dumpling nights are another way to meet people.
catchers.confirm: Are you looking for casual evening conversation in Cantonese rather than paid tutoring or professional services?

forbids.text: I cannot discuss any court case or anything I learn in my interpreting work.
I'm unavailable during weekday court hours.
I won't take interpreting work paying under $35 an hour.
I protect my Thursday evening pottery class and won't book over it.
I won't record or share my grandmother's words without her consent.

projects.name: Taishanese story and word archive
projects.text: Recording my grandmother's stories and Taishanese words before they are lost, with transcription and translation.

projects.name: Spring trip to Taishan with my grandmother
projects.text: A possible trip to Guangzhou and Taishan next spring, if my grandmother is well enough and agrees.

policy.t1: When there is a real sign of a fit, I'll share that my bookings have fallen and I have free evenings, my availability, my glossaries and training experience, and the Taishanese recording idea.
policy.t2: Once trust is clear and the other person is known, I'll share my family situation, including the bakery and my grandmother, and my worries about the trip.
policy.never: Details of any court case, and my personal finances.
